paragraphs: Matching problems depend on knowing which outcomes users prefer, but collecting that information can demand considerable effort from them. This paper addresses both learning preferences and deciding which preference questions to ask next. Its central idea is that query selection should reflect the objective of the matching problem.

The authors introduce a method for determining probabilistic matchings and develop several active learning strategies that are sensitive to the matching objective. This connects the treatment of uncertainty with the decision the system ultimately needs to make. A preference question is therefore considered in relation to its usefulness for matching, giving query selection a more specific purpose than learning preferences in isolation.

Experiments on real-world datasets from diverse domains show that these matching-sensitive strategies outperform standard techniques. The stated finding supports tailoring active learning to the downstream decision. For applications that require users to express preferences, the contribution is an approach designed to make those interactions more useful while reducing the amount of information users must supply.
icml-2012-active-learning-for-matching-p.tldr: Matching-aware active learning selects preference questions around the matching objective and outperforms standard techniques in experiments.

paragraphs: Learning a distribution over model parameters allows a method to represent uncertainty about those parameters. Extending this idea from weight vectors to matrices creates a substantial storage problem: for a matrix with dimension n, a full covariance description requires a number of parameters proportional to n to the fourth power. This paper develops two ways to make such matrix models manageable.

The first algorithm keeps only a diagonal covariance, providing a simpler uncertainty representation that can handle large parameter collections. The second factors the covariance, retaining some correlations between features while keeping the parameter count linear in the size of the original matrix. These are different compromises between the richness of the uncertainty model and the cost of maintaining it.

The authors analyze the diagonal method through a mistake bound and evaluate their approach on similar-image retrieval and similar-document ranking. They report better precision than competing algorithms on these tasks. The factored algorithm is also shown to converge faster, supporting the usefulness of retaining some correlation information without constructing the full covariance.
icml-2012-adaptive-regularization-for-si.tldr: Two compact covariance representations make learning distributions over similarity matrices practical, with improved precision and faster convergence reported.

paragraphs: Boosting aims to combine weak learners into a stronger learner. This paper considers the online version of that task, in which the component learners and their combination operate as learning proceeds. The motivation is a gap in theoretical understanding: batch boosting already has a sound foundation, while the online setting has received less theoretical support.

The authors propose an online boosting algorithm and establish a theoretical guarantee for it. The contribution therefore goes beyond introducing another combination procedure: it supplies formal justification within the online setting itself. That matters because the paper's stated goal is to understand how weak online learners can support a strong online learner, rather than relying only on the established theory for batch learning.

The paper also evaluates the algorithm on real-world datasets and reports favorable comparisons with existing algorithms. These experiments provide practical evidence alongside the theoretical result. Together, the two parts support the proposed method as an online boosting approach with both formal backing and encouraging observed performance.
icml-2012-an-online-boosting-algorithm-w.tldr: The paper introduces an online boosting algorithm with a theoretical guarantee and favorable results on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Two time series are cointegrated when a linear combination of them is stationary, meaning that the combination has stable statistical behavior over time. The conventional test first estimates a linear relationship using ordinary least squares and then tests its residuals for a unit root. The paper identifies erroneous conclusions about cointegration as a known weakness of this two-stage procedure.

The authors replace that workflow with a coherent Bayesian framework for estimating whether cointegration exists. The relationship between the series and the assessment of cointegration are handled within this framework. Their empirical comparison finds the Bayesian approach superior to the classical procedure, supporting it as an alternative for assessing this particular kind of relationship between time series.

The framework is also applied to segmented cointegration, where the relationship may hold only during limited periods. This extends the question from whether cointegration exists to how its presence can vary over time. Unlike previous approaches discussed in the abstract, the model places no restriction on the number of possible cointegration segments.
icml-2012-bayesian-conditional-cointegra.tldr: A Bayesian framework improves empirical cointegration assessment and models relationships that hold across an unrestricted number of time segments.

paragraphs: Describing a topic through its most frequent words captures what appears often, but does not fully capture what distinguishes that topic. A word can be common within one topic while also appearing broadly elsewhere. This paper treats exclusivity, or how specifically a word belongs to a topic, as equally important for communicating topical content.

The proposed Hierarchical Poisson Convolution model estimates both word frequency within topics and differences in word use across topics. Its estimates are regularized, placing constraints on how freely they can vary. The model uses a known hierarchy of human-labeled topics to focus comparisons within individual branches, so differences in usage are examined in relation to the supplied topic structure.

This approach makes topic description depend on both prevalence and distinctiveness. Its reliance on a known hierarchy is a concrete part of the method: the structure guides which comparisons receive attention. The authors also develop a parallel Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampler, providing the computational machinery they describe as enabling fast and scalable estimation.
icml-2012-capturing-topical-content-with.tldr: Hierarchical Poisson Convolution describes topics using both word frequency and distinctiveness, guided by a known hierarchy of labeled topics.

paragraphs: Supervised dimensionality reduction seeks a smaller representation that preserves information useful for identifying classes. This paper studies linear projections from an information-theoretic perspective. It chooses the projection by maximizing mutual information between the projected observations and their class labels, using Shannon entropy to define that information.

The central computational contribution is a way to optimize this objective directly. The authors use a theoretical result giving the gradient of mutual information, allowing gradient descent without simplifying the objective function. This matters because the quantity being optimized remains the stated measure of class-relevant information, rather than a simplified replacement introduced to make optimization easier.

The paper provides theoretical and empirical comparisons with Linear Discriminant Analysis and Information Discriminant Analysis. It also compares against a related approach based on Renyi entropy, whose gradient is simple under a particular parameter setting. Results on real datasets are described as promising relative to these alternatives. The contribution combines a principled projection objective with a direct optimization route and encouraging empirical evidence.
icml-2012-communications-inspired-linear.tldr: The method learns linear projections by directly optimizing Shannon mutual information with class labels, producing promising results on real datasets.

paragraphs: Differentially private estimation introduces randomness to protect information about the data, creating a tradeoff among privacy, accuracy, and sample size. This paper studies how accurately private procedures can approximate statistical estimators as more data become available. It establishes both upper and lower bounds, addressing achievable performance as well as barriers to improvement.

The key finding connects private estimation with B-robustness, a property from robust statistics. Over a large class of distributions, an estimator that lacks this property cannot be approximated well under differential privacy. The scope of that statement matters: it identifies an obstacle to broad approximation guarantees, rather than asserting that every particular estimation problem must be difficult.

For a B-robust estimator whose output range is bounded, the authors provide an upper bound on the convergence rate of a private approximation. They also show that the bounded-range condition is necessary for the strict form of differential privacy they consider. Together, these results make robustness and output range central to understanding which private approximation guarantees are possible.
icml-2012-convergence-rates-for-differen.tldr: The paper links private estimation rates to B-robustness and establishes the role of bounded estimator ranges under strict differential privacy.

paragraphs: Dynamic topic modeling represents topical content together with its changing structure. This paper develops dependent hierarchical normalized random measures for that purpose. The main modeling idea is to connect the underlying random measures, giving the topic model a probabilistic mechanism for dependency rather than treating its components as unrelated.

The dependencies are constructed through superposition, subsampling, and transitions of points in underlying Poisson processes. These operations combine processes, select parts of them, and move their points. The family includes normalized generalized Gamma processes with power-law properties, which the authors distinguish from the Dirichlet processes previously used for dynamic topic modeling. This expands the kinds of statistical behavior available to the model.

For inference, the authors adapt a slice sampler to work directly with the underlying Poisson process. Experiments span news, blogs, academic material, and Twitter collections. The method achieves better perplexity than several previous models on those collections. The reported evidence therefore supports improved probabilistic modeling of text across multiple sources, alongside the new construction of dependent measures.
icml-2012-dependent-hierarchical-normali.tldr: Dependent random measures with power-law properties support dynamic topic models that improve perplexity over several previous models.

paragraphs: Some supervised learning problems describe each input as a collection of feature vectors rather than a single vector. Their target labels may also be soft, expressing class probabilities instead of one definite class. This paper proposes a representation-learning method that accommodates both features of this setting through probabilistic prototype patterns.

An input is represented using a mixture of probabilities over its feature vectors. Each probability expresses how likely a vector is to belong to an unknown prototype pattern. Hidden variables parameterize those patterns, making likelihood-based training possible. Crucially, the prototypes and the other model parameters can both be learned discriminatively, so the representation is shaped by the supervised prediction task.

The authors show that the model is a probabilistic generalization of learning vector quantization. They evaluate it on shape classification, hyperspectral image classification, and categorization of people's work classes. Across these applications, they report superior performance relative to a standard prototype classifier and other competitive methods. The findings support learning task-sensitive probabilistic prototypes for inputs composed of sets of vectors.
icml-2012-discriminative-probabilistic-p.tldr: The method learns probabilistic prototypes discriminatively for set-valued inputs, supporting soft labels and improving classification in the reported applications.

paragraphs: A classifier built from many base classifiers can spend substantial computation evaluating them. This paper constructs a sparse directed acyclic decision graph from a list supplied by another learning method, such as AdaBoost. The graph selects which base classifiers to evaluate according to the particular input being processed.

The authors formulate graph design as a Markov decision process. At each stage, the system decides whether to use or skip a base classifier based on its current classification state. This turns computation into a sequence of input-dependent decisions. A single hyperparameter controls the tradeoff between speed and accuracy, giving the user an explicit way to choose how much computation to spend.

On three object-detection benchmarks, the method is competitive with state-of-the-art cascades and clearly better when few base classifiers are used. It also applies readily to multiclass classification. In a web-page ranking experiment using that setup, the authors report substantially faster decisions without harming ranking performance, illustrating a practical benefit of selectively evaluating the available classifiers.
icml-2012-fast-classification-using-spar.tldr: Sparse decision graphs speed classification by learning when each input should use or skip base classifiers.

paragraphs: Feature selection requires a way to judge which input variables are informative for prediction. This paper studies two scoring criteria that use estimated class probabilities: an existing method and a complementary method introduced by the authors. The focus is on understanding what these probability-based scores actually measure and when one is preferable.

The theoretical analysis shows that both criteria estimate the spread of the probability of belonging to the positive class across a feature's possible values. In plain language, they examine how much the estimated chance of a positive label changes as the feature changes. This gives the scores a shared interpretation while leaving room for differences in how effectively they capture that variation.

The authors use this framework to predict conditions under which each scoring method should have an advantage over the other. Empirical results validate those predictions. The contribution is therefore both a complementary feature score and an explanation of comparative behavior, providing a basis for choosing between the two criteria rather than treating either as universally superior.
icml-2012-feature-selection-via-probabil.tldr: Two probability-based feature scores measure variation in positive-class probability, and theory predicts when each has an advantage.

paragraphs: Quantile regression estimates a chosen point in the distribution of a response as a function of the inputs. This allows the prediction target to be a particular quantile, rather than only a central average. The paper develops a direct quantile regression framework using a Gaussian process model.

The model is learned by minimizing expected tilted loss, the objective associated here with estimating the desired quantile. Learning requires an integration that cannot be performed analytically. The authors employ Expectation Propagation to address that computational obstacle and speed up learning. The approximation is thus part of making the proposed probabilistic framework computationally usable.

The paper also explains how the framework relates to other quantile regression methods and applies it to synthetic and real datasets. These applications demonstrate use of the method in both controlled and observed-data settings. The central contribution is the combination of Gaussian process modeling, a quantile-focused learning objective, and an inference procedure that handles the otherwise intractable integration.
icml-2012-gaussian-process-quantile-regr.tldr: A Gaussian process framework estimates response quantiles using expected tilted loss and Expectation Propagation for tractable learning.

paragraphs: Prior causal knowledge can say that one variable affects another, or that no such effect exists, without specifying a direct connection. This paper represents those statements as constraints on directed paths. That formulation accommodates indirect causal relationships, including knowledge obtained from experiments.

The authors develop procedures for incorporating these constraints into Causal Bayesian Networks and Maximal Ancestral Graphs, as well as the graph representations of their Markov equivalence classes. They establish soundness and completeness for the procedures. Within the formalisms studied, these properties provide formal support for both the validity of the resulting inferences and the procedures' ability to incorporate the relevant implications of the supplied knowledge.

Simulations show that even a small number of causal facts often yields many additional inferences. A biological case study demonstrates the full route from real experimental data to causal knowledge and then into an existing causal network. The contribution shows how information about causal reachability can constrain a model beyond the individual relationships initially supplied.
icml-2012-incorporating-causal-prior-kno.tldr: Sound and complete procedures incorporate direct or indirect causal knowledge as path constraints, often enabling many additional inferences.

paragraphs: Finding the maximum of a high-dimensional, nonconvex function is difficult when observations are noisy. This paper models the unknown function as a sample from a Gaussian process distribution. Its crucial assumption is that only a small subset of the available variables actually influences the function.

Under that assumption, the authors develop an algorithm that combines variable selection with Gaussian process optimization. The task is to identify which inputs matter while also searching for good function values. Combining these goals addresses the mismatch between a large input space and a function whose behavior depends on relatively few coordinates.

The theoretical results bound the number of observations needed for variable selection and provide cumulative regret bounds for optimization. These guarantees address both discovering relevant variables and the accumulated cost of making suboptimal choices during the search. Experiments on several benchmark optimization problems also support the algorithm's effectiveness. The result is a conditional route to high-dimensional optimization, with sparsity in the relevant variables providing the central simplifying structure.
icml-2012-joint-optimization-and-variabl.tldr: Assuming few relevant variables, the algorithm jointly selects inputs and optimizes a noisy Gaussian process function with theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Structured sparse coding seeks representations with a constrained pattern of active components, but obtaining those representations through iterative optimization can be expensive. This paper develops a framework for replacing that repeated computation with learned fast encoders. It extends approaches that train regressors to approximate exact sparse codes.

The authors first introduce a block-coordinate proximal splitting method for hierarchical sparse coding. They then derive an efficient feedforward architecture from an iteration of that method. This connects the learned encoder to the underlying optimization procedure. The resulting architecture closely approximates structured sparse codes using a fraction of the complexity of standard optimization methods.

Different training objectives also allow the encoders to act as sparse representation learners or modelers, beyond reproducing codes for a fixed dictionary. A simple implementation achieves speedups of several orders of magnitude over the state of the art with minimal performance degradation. These reported results support the framework's suitability for real-time and large-scale uses where repeatedly solving the original optimization problem would be costly.
icml-2012-learning-efficient-structured-.tldr: Optimization-derived feedforward encoders produce structured sparse representations with reported orders-of-magnitude speedups and minimal performance loss.

paragraphs: Extracting information from text often focuses on isolated facts, such as recognizing that a named place is a city. Such facts help organize knowledge, but they do not describe how events and their participants fit together. This talk motivates unsupervised approaches for learning that richer structure from unlabeled text.

The abstract distinguishes atomic relations from connections among events. A bomb detonation can be related to a building's destruction, while a person's conviction can imply an earlier arrest. Understanding these connections involves representing more than individual words or standalone assertions: it requires a structured account of events, the entities involved, and relationships across those events.

The stated approach is to learn this richer knowledge without labeled examples, making unlabeled text the source of structure. Its significance lies in broadening what information extraction aims to recover. Instead of stopping with a collection of separate facts, the work seeks representations that support a deeper account of what happened and who participated, with the aim of helping intelligent systems organize textual knowledge.
icml-2012-learning-the-central-events-an.tldr: The talk describes unsupervised approaches to learning structured relationships among events and participants from unlabeled text.

paragraphs: Multiple views of data can contain both common information and variation specific to each view. This paper introduces a fully Bayesian latent variable model that separates those sources into shared and private representations. It uses conditional nonlinear dependence and independence structure to learn an efficient hidden description of the observations.

Bayesian techniques automatically estimate the dimensions of the latent spaces. The model can work directly with extremely high-dimensional observations, including high-resolution images. In an ambiguous human-pose prediction task, priors incorporating the dynamics of the data allow the representation to resolve ambiguity in a principled way. This connects uncertainty in the representation with structural knowledge about how the data evolve.

A facial-image demonstration shows the model learning a low-dimensional representation under different lighting conditions. It automatically places lighting variation in a separate latent space from variation associated with different faces. The model also generates morphed faces and images under novel light directions, illustrating how the learned separation can support synthesis as well as representation.
icml-2012-manifold-relevance-determinati.tldr: A Bayesian latent model automatically separates shared and private variation, estimates latent dimensions, and supports disambiguation and image generation.

paragraphs: Denoising autoencoders learn representations by reconstructing inputs after some of their information has been corrupted. Stacking these models had produced strong sentiment-analysis results for domain adaptation, where a representation must remain useful across domains. This paper seeks to retain that benefit while greatly reducing the cost of learning the representation.

The proposed marginalized stacked denoising autoencoder explicitly averages out the feature corruption and solves for its parameters in closed form. It therefore avoids training through backpropagation. The central change is computational: the corruption remains part of the learning formulation, but its effect is handled analytically instead of requiring the original training procedure.

The authors report comparable accuracy to the original approach while reducing computation on large datasets from several days to minutes. They also describe an implementation requiring only twenty lines of MATLAB. These findings make the method significant as a simpler and faster way to obtain useful domain-adaptation representations, preserving the reported accuracy level while substantially lowering the practical cost of training.
icml-2012-marginalized-denoising-autoenc.tldr: Marginalizing feature corruption enables closed-form denoising autoencoder training, retaining comparable accuracy while reducing reported training time from days to minutes.

paragraphs: Polyphonic music contains multiple notes at the same time, making each step in a symbolic sequence a high-dimensional observation. This paper studies that setting using a general piano-roll representation. The learning problem is to capture how these complex musical observations depend on what has occurred earlier in the sequence.

The authors introduce a probabilistic model whose distribution estimators are conditioned on a recurrent neural network. The recurrent component provides temporal context, while the distribution estimators model the high-dimensional observations. This arrangement gives the model a way to discover temporal dependencies in sequences with richer individual steps than a single symbol.

On a variety of realistic datasets, the approach outperforms many traditional polyphonic music models. The authors also use the learned musical language model as a symbolic prior for polyphonic transcription and show improved transcription accuracy. This second result demonstrates that modeling symbolic musical structure can help an associated prediction task: the learned dependencies provide information that improves the reconstruction of the notes.
icml-2012-modeling-temporal-dependencies.tldr: A recurrently conditioned probabilistic model learns polyphonic music dependencies and improves transcription when used as a symbolic prior.

paragraphs: Online learning usually compares a learner's performance with the best hypothesis chosen after seeing all the data. For some hypothesis classes, however, even finding that best hypothesis offline is difficult. This paper proposes local regret as a benchmark aligned with settings where local search and local optimality are more practical.

Local regret compares performance with nearby hypotheses rather than requiring comparison with the global best. A locality graph defines which hypotheses count as neighbors. The authors present a general algorithm that can minimize local regret for arbitrary such graphs. They also show that particular graph structures can make the learning procedure substantially simpler.

The algorithms are demonstrated on online disjunct learning, online Max-SAT, and online decision tree learning, including some previously unexplored online problems. The contribution changes what successful online learning asks for when global optimization is challenging. Its guarantee concerns the chosen neighborhood structure, making the definition of locality an essential part of both the learning objective and the opportunities for computational simplification.
icml-2012-on-local-regret-e9219927e8.tldr: Local regret benchmarks online learning against nearby hypotheses, with algorithms for arbitrary locality graphs and simplifications for structured graphs.

paragraphs: Dynamic decision-making often needs to account for variability as well as average outcomes. Variance-related risk criteria make that concern explicit, but optimizing many such criteria is NP-hard. This paper develops a framework for local policy-gradient reinforcement learning methods that incorporate both expected cost and its variance.

The starting point is a new expression for the variance of cost-to-go in episodic tasks. Cost-to-go describes the remaining accumulated cost, so its variance captures uncertainty in that accumulated outcome. The authors use this formula to derive policy-gradient algorithms for objectives involving both the mean and variability of cost, connecting a risk-sensitive objective to a policy update procedure.

The paper proves that the algorithms converge to local minima and demonstrates their applicability in portfolio planning. The local nature of the guarantee is central: the result establishes convergence to locally optimal solutions within a difficult optimization setting. The contribution provides a formally supported way to learn policies for variance-related objectives while addressing risk directly in the learning criterion.
icml-2012-policy-gradients-with-variance.tldr: A new episodic cost-variance formula supports risk-sensitive policy-gradient algorithms with proven convergence to local minima.

paragraphs: Training a kernel support vector machine requires an optimization procedure, so the computational behavior of that procedure is part of making the learning method useful. This paper introduces a new training approach called the Kernelized Stochastic Batch Perceptron. Its central subject is the efficiency of learning kernel SVMs.

The authors establish learning-runtime guarantees that are better than those of any other kernelized SVM optimization approach known in the comparison they state. This is a theoretical claim about the proposed method's runtime guarantees. The significance is that the paper supports its efficiency argument through analysis of the learning procedure, giving a formal basis for comparing it with existing optimization approaches.

The paper also reports that the method works well in practice relative to existing alternatives. That practical finding complements the theoretical contribution without making an unrestricted claim that every training run will be faster. Taken together, the stated results present a new kernel SVM training method backed by stronger runtime guarantees and favorable practical comparisons.
icml-2012-the-kernelized-stochastic-batc.tldr: The Kernelized Stochastic Batch Perceptron trains kernel SVMs with stronger stated learning-runtime guarantees and favorable practical performance.

paragraphs: Restricted Boltzmann machines can model complex observations, but word data create a computational bottleneck. Each word is a discrete choice from a vocabulary that may contain hundreds of thousands of entries. Conventional block Gibbs training samples from visible softmax units with a cost that grows linearly with vocabulary size.

The authors replace those visible-unit updates with a more general class of Markov chain Monte Carlo operators. The resulting update complexity is independent of vocabulary size. This targets the costly sampling operation directly, making larger vocabularies feasible without the same vocabulary-dependent cost for each such update.

The method is demonstrated by training on hundreds of millions of word n-grams with vocabularies larger than previously feasible. The learned features improve performance on chunking and sentiment classification, with state-of-the-art results reported for sentiment classification. These findings connect the computational change to useful learned representations: the approach supports larger-scale word modeling and yields features that benefit downstream language tasks.
icml-2012-training-restricted-boltzmann-.tldr: Alternative Monte Carlo updates remove vocabulary-size dependence from RBM visible-unit updates and enable useful large-scale word representations.

paragraphs: Manifold learning seeks an underlying geometric representation of data, but spectral kernel eigenmap methods can be sensitive to noise. This paper addresses that difficulty when the same data have two related views. Instead of reconstructing each view separately, it treats the two manifold-learning problems as interconnected.

The proposed algorithms use spectral decomposition of cross-covariance operators in Hilbert space. In plain language, they extract structure from the relationship between the two views. Each view can help suppress noise in the other, reducing bias and allowing the joint approach to succeed in situations where a non-integrated approach would fail. The usefulness of the connection between views is central to this argument.

The authors discuss when two-manifold problems are useful and demonstrate an application to learning a nonlinear dynamical system from limited data. This shows a role for joint geometric reconstruction beyond representing a static dataset. The contribution is a class of algorithms that uses related views as mutual sources of information for recovering structure in noisy observations.
icml-2012-two-manifold-problems-with-app.tldr: Jointly learning two related manifolds lets each view suppress noise in the other and can aid nonlinear system identification.

paragraphs: Precision-recall curves and their areas are widely used to summarize machine learning performance, especially when class proportions are uneven. Their behavior is often interpreted by analogy with ROC curves. This paper examines a structural feature of precision-recall space that affects how those summaries should be understood.

It was already known that precision-recall curves change when class skew changes. The paper identifies an additional fact: an entire region of precision-recall space is impossible to achieve, and the size of that region depends only on class skew. The authors precisely characterize its size, separating a constraint imposed by class proportions from differences attributable to the evaluated method.

This matters for empirical evaluation because the space in which performance is measured changes with the class balance. A curve or area therefore sits within a feasible region whose geometry is partly determined by the dataset. The paper discusses the methodological implications of this constraint, providing a more precise basis for interpreting precision-recall results in settings with different class proportions.
icml-2012-unachievable-region-in-precisi.tldr: Precision-recall space contains an impossible region whose size depends only on class skew, affecting interpretation of evaluation results.
